blocks.x: I guess it's working all right. I mentioned that this is Bill Russell and Ralph Collins interviewing Mr. Robinson and we're over at this is 1811 Terpsichore. Do you mind giving your full name? My name is Joseph Ralph Robinson. Middle name is Ralph. Do you mind telling just when you were born and where it was? Yeah. What was the date of your birthday? September 12, 1884. 1884. So you're 77 you say now? Yes. Were you born right here in the city? No. I was born in the country.
New Road, Louisiana. Where is that? Up the river? About 122 miles from here. Which way is that?
Going up from here. Near Baton Rouge? Yeah. Yeah. When did you move down here? Do you remember how old you were about?
Yeah I got a half a dollar. Oh really? The time I moved 18, let me see. I don't want a line mistake. Let me see 1912.

1912. 1912. Yeah. Not many years since. Been moving from place to place. Yeah. Yesterday when Lemonash came with the, when we picked up your violin, you mentioned you bought that violin when you were 18 years old.
18 years old. Yeah. Yeah. Where were you then? I was in a place they called, uh, Chennau. It's from, uh, about, about 25 miles from New Road.
Up, up, upstate then. That's right. Uh, were you playing, uh, music at that time? Was that your first instrument? When did you, what instrument did you start on?

Me? Me? Yes. On, uh, violin. The violin came before the clarinet then? Yeah. After that I used to play in different, uh, bands, you know? Yes. With this one sometime, this one, this one, they'd come at me sometime, I'd hide from it. Yeah. I would stop going, uh, going out, you know?
Oh, well. Yes. Can you tell us about the, your lessons you mentioned yesterday? You had some lessons with, uh, old professor Jim Humphrey.
Humphrey, yes. Did you take any other lessons before that? No, sir, I hadn't. Only with Jim Humphrey.
When you started on the violin, did you have lessons right away on that, or? No, I didn't have no lesson. I didn't play.

Picked it up? Yeah, I just picked it up myself, but, uh, but Jim Humphrey was teaching, teaching me clarinet, you know? Well, he's the one who taught you clarinet then? After he died, I gave up all things, you know? Yeah. Yeah. But I used to write my own music and bring to him, you know? And he, you know, divided, you know?
Yes. You mentioned that you heard some, uh, music on the, uh, phonograph, the graphophone? Oh, yeah. I used to have a graphophone, you know?
I'd put it there, you know? Play a while and stop and write a while, you know? Yeah. And, and play it a while again and stop, you know?
Do you remember what pieces those were and what the band was that you heard playing?
No. I can't remember them pieces. It's been so long. Oh, yeah. It's been a long time. Yeah, and I never did bother with it after the old man passed out, you know?
Yeah. That's the, that music you would take up to Professor Humphrey, you told me yesterday.

Yeah, only, yeah. Only him. I took lessons from him. Only him. Now, the name of the little band was Forest River Band, you know? Forest River Band. Of course, River. That was the name of your band? Yeah, band, yeah. We had six pieces, I think. Two guitar, bass violin, cornet, and violin. That makes five, I guess. Did you bass two guitars? Yeah, but I wasn't playing my music, though.
Did they have any trombone in the band ever? No, no. We didn't have any. No piano then, either? No piano, no. No piano.

Or was there a clarinet at that time? Yeah. No clarinet. No clarinet either? No clarinet. Just a cornet, violin, two guitar, and a bass violin. Almost a string band, wasn't it? Two guitar, yeah, yeah, string band. We were petering at this fella, Joe Scott, you know, in Natchez. No. No, I don't think so. Old Buddy, Buddy, you? No, I don't believe. Buddy Scott, from Natchez, Mississippi. Buddy Scott? Yeah, Buddy Scott. Oh, Buddy Scott. Oh, Buddy Scott. Oh, sure. Yeah, Buddy Scott. Yeah, Buddy Scott. Yeah, I knew him. Yeah, I knew him. He's dead now. Yeah, he used to sit, take two chairs. He's so big. Was he that big in those days? Yeah, that's right. Yeah, he was pretty big when I knew him. Yeah, he was big for him. Oh, no, I didn't know who you meant. Bud Scott, I forgot. Bud Scott, yeah. I forgot about him. Did he play with you, you say, Mr. No, I didn't play with them. No. But I... But you patterned the band. Yeah. Yeah. I used to even call my guitar, one of my guitar boys, Bud Scott. You did too? Yeah. Bud Scott. Sometimes they'd go wrong, you know, and hit him with my violin. Yeah.
I didn't know he was from Natchez. Oh, yeah. Yeah, Natchez, Mississippi.
Yeah, I knew he came from that. Yeah.
Yeah.
Bud Scott. He had some bands, those string bands. Yeah, some big. And it's another fella.
How many did he have in his band? About the same like your group?

About, I guess. I never did see them, yeah, but I often heard them play, you know. In different places they'd go, but I never did go, and my boys would come back and tell me, you know. Yeah. And so I used to call one of the guitar players, Bud Scott, but his name was Frank Sheese. It's your TZ. That was your guitar player? Yeah. Yeah.
I might be the guitar player. Buddy Scott's band, where was it playing at that time? Was it in the city or?
Yeah, it used to go about, you know. Oh, I see. Around Natchez, huh? Yeah, yeah. On Natchez. Up that section, Mississippi. From Natchez, yeah. Natchez, Mississippi.
I see. He wasn't playing in the city steady. No, no, no, no.

And you were up in the country too? Yeah, I was in the country, you know. Yeah. In a place they call, uh, Chanel. Yeah. Chanel from New Road, about 20, 20 some odd mile, coming from New Road. They call it, uh, up, coming this way, you know. Yeah. Yeah. And so, so I used to call my boy, Bud Scott. We play all in LaVonia, only for white folks, you know. We play for concerts, such as, uh, concerts and dances and everything. We had a little rig, you know, with two horses. Oh, is it? Yeah. We used to go out there, yeah. A place they called, LaVonia, Falls River, a little station, you know.
You got the whole band, didn't they?
Yeah, oh yeah. We used to go. But they'd always write to me, you know.
Yeah. You were the manager and leader.
Tell them, yeah. Tell them how to do.
Do you remember what kind of music you used? Any of the pieces or what kind of, uh, some kind of dance music, of course. Was it mostly for dance? You said concerts, though, too, didn't you?

Yeah, for dance, for dance, sometimes for dance. We went play in a place they called Fudo's once. They had a band there they called McGrudy. They was playing, you know. But after we come in there, you know, they stopped and, oh. Oh yeah. I wanted to hear your band. Yeah, but they had piano and everything in there. They could play alright. I listened to them good, you know. And I know good music when they played it, you know. And so, we'd play for them. We'd come back with a loaded outfit, you know, such as whiskey and all things that we didn't need. We'd stop at all them stores and fellows would play us down, you know. Mm-hmm. To play for them. You know. We'd stop there and play a piece for them. Give us whiskey and everything. We'd load it in the little rig, you know. Two horses. And sometime we'd come back, like before day, in the morning. We'd play a little chord, but just amongst us fellas, you know. We didn't mix up with no other, you know. Just with us boys. We'd play some time. Five-up, seven. Five-up and this game they called, uh, uh, pitty pair, you know. Those are all card games or what? Yeah. Yeah. We just, uh, playing with cards. Yeah, yeah. We didn't mix up with no other fellas. Yeah.
Can you tell me anything more about the music? What kind of dancing they had in those days? Were they waltzes or two steps or foxtrot or quadrille or what kind of music was it?

Oh, waltzes, foxtrot, different things. And the gallops. Gallops. Oh, yeah. All such things is that. Some want this one. Some want to dance this one. Oh, they, they used to kick about the music. We played so nice, you know. And so, them boys, they died out. And so I gave them. And we'd bother with it no more. And that's been a long time. Never did bother with it no more. When did you take up the clarinet, Mr. Robinson? The clarinet? I just picked up on that myself. I could play it too, boy.
How old were you about when you picked up on that? Huh? How old were you?

I was about, let me see, about, about fifty, fifty-someone. About fifty-year-old. Oh, then? Yeah, that's all the time. You weren't a young boy anymore. No. I used to play it too, I'll tell you. But I was playing by, you know. I didn't like it well, you know, playing by, but then I learned it like this after the professor gave up, you know, the teaching. I used to write my own music and bring there, you divide it, you know. Oh, yeah.
Well, you'd be just young though then. Yeah, I was a young fella. How old would you be when you took up the violin? Well...

You said eighteen, you told me yesterday, you bought the violin. Yeah, eighteen, I bought the violin. Had you played before that? From a fella, that violin you took, you got there. Yeah. I bought it from a fella named, uh, Fair Charles. In a place they call Livonia, Louisiana. Livonia. We had a railroad, uh, we had a railroad, uh, stage. He had a stool just on this side, the railroad, you know. Yeah. And I used to go there, he had two. And so, I asked him once. I had one, I had a violin myself, you know. Yeah. But one of them got broke up. One of my violin got all broke up. How long had you been playing before you bought this one? Hmm. Well, I hadn't long started playing there. I hadn't long. Hadn't been going very long. Very long, you know. Mm-hmm. And used to go by playing out there toward them, you know. And I stopped in the store once. Yeah. And there was, we made a bargain. Yeah. And that violin, what, what I sold to you, it cost me $16. He had two. Mm-hmm. And you know how people lit up. Yeah. He had a little small one and a big one. Yeah. And I said, I want the big one. Yeah, sure. That's the one you got. I got the big one. It was $16. He had two. Yeah, that's been quite a while.
When you took up the clarinet, you say you just played by ear? You didn't live?
Yeah, I did. No, I never did play ball music. I started with a... But with Mr. Umphrey. Umphrey, yeah. And after...
Can you tell us about his lessons? Where did he teach? At his home or did he come to your house?
At his home. At his home. At his home. Grew uptown there. On Kidders Street. Oh, yeah. In Robeson, I think it was. Yeah.
His, uh, his, uh, grandchildren, some of them live up that way. Yeah.
The same, almost the same place, I think. Yeah. On Kidders Street.
Just about the same place, I guess.
In Robeson, I think. Let me see. Yeah.
Except they're pretty close. Yeah.
Pretty close, yeah. Where they are. But I used to go to them, you know. I couldn't even...
You remember how much he... How much did he charge for lessons, you remember, in those days? No, no. I don't know. He just...
He charged me, you know, about a week. So, you know. That's what I wanted, you know.
About how often... How often did you go there? More than once a week, or? About twice a week. About twice a week.

Yeah. And he teach me, my lesson. He said, you such a good scholar, say. Rob, sorry. I need to charge you anything. Said, you got somebody giving you, uh, some ideas about them. I said, no. I said, well, let me tell you one thing, Professor. I said, if I had anybody else to teach me anything, I wouldn't come to you. Yeah. It would be no use to be coming to you. Yeah. If I had to let somebody else tell me what to do, I want you to teach me.
Sure.

He said, well, that's good. I said, first and last, I guess I'll catch you on Jack Carey and them. You know, one musician, they used to back... They wag your tail together, you know, and play. I said, next time, but Rousin and Mark, remember what I'm telling you. If I catch you on the bed where, uh, with Jack Carey, they're playing out in the street like that. Don't come to me, no. I said, no, I don't go to them. You didn't like that kind of music, huh?
No, I didn't. I did not. I mean, he didn't, uh, old Jim Humphrey didn't like that? He didn't like that either. Oh, no, he didn't like that. He didn't, huh? No, he didn't.

And I appreciated it. I didn't like it, but I said, playing out, you know, in the street. Yeah. And so we used to have a little band. We used to rehearse at a place they called, uh, right here in this city. And, uh, place they called, uh, it's a church. They got a school there, I think. Right downtown there on Tulane Avenue, I think. We were in that vicinity. And, uh, we used to play, and the boys all, you know, they used to come in the back of me, I was playing, uh, the first client. Is that near, yeah. Is that near Charity Hospital?
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
There's a hall there they call it St. Catherine.
St. Catherine. Is that it?
St. Catherine. Is that it?

Exactly, that's the place. I know the other one. Well, we used to go there and everybody, everybody stand in the back of me, you know, see if I'm reading this right, you know. And they said, it's doggone, I used to play at them partners, you know. I was in the band with them there, a pretty two-piece band, I think. And I used to play a clannin. And they all would stand in the back of me all the time, see. I used to be glad that, you know.
Did you have any book when you took lessons from Professor Umphrey? I had a big book, yeah. I don't know what become of it, yeah. You don't remember the name of it?
Yeah, let me see, I don't know if I got the name.
Was it a method book?

Method book, yeah, exactly, yeah. I had some of his pieces. And he wrote them? Yeah, yeah. That he wrote out? And I just tore them up, you know. I said, sure, I don't think that'll be any good for me anymore.
Yeah, I wish we could find some of them. Yeah, yeah, that's all right. We'd like to have them. Put them in our library up at Tulane now, if we could find something like that.

I had some good done, a marching thing, you know. Like all the soldier boys and all such is that, you know. Yeah. And music. Let me see. I don't think I saved any of them things. And pieces. Yeah, I had a gang of them. I had even a book. I don't know what I did with them. They're not even here. I don't think I put them up anywhere, you know where I could get them. If you'd ever find something like that, we'd be glad to buy it from you too and tell you to. I'd be glad for you to have it. Searching around, I might look and find something.
You might find something like that. I'll stop someday in a few months.
Maybe you'll come across it sometime. I'd like for you to stop.
Yeah, I'd look around.

Things are still clustered up, you know. Yeah, I know how it is. My place is the same thing. Yeah, look at things. I've got things stuck up everywhere. Yeah, that's right. Do you have any photographs of your old bands? No. The band, your own band that you played up in the country or down here? No, I haven't got none of them.
To get back to the St. Catherine's Hall over there, did you play any dances there or what was that?
No, we used to the Royce. That was it, the big brass band?
Yeah, big band.

Big brass band. Mostly all foreigners, you know, from Belize. Something like that, yeah. Belize. All foreigners. And they used to be sticky to me, you know. They used to like me. And they'd play so good in a clad tone. You know, I had a good clad in a clad tone. I put that clarinet in the shop and never did get my clarinet back. Well, that's when you lost at Goonwals. Yeah. When Goonwals moved. And I paid just $27 for it, you know. Yeah. I paid $27 for it. I don't forget the name of it. It was almost new then. New, yeah.

I remember if it could have been a buffet or Selmer or... No. Is it a French clarinet, do you think? It was made in Paris. Made in Paris. Yeah. Maybe Pencil Moller or something like that. Well, it might have been a buffet, but you don't know.

Yeah, it could be. Yeah, no, I never did notice the name on it. Yeah. Of course the name be on the barrel of it, you know. Yeah. I never did notice. I remember a fella had a clarinet. He bought it. And it was cold that night. We were re-oist. And when we got through there, we were putting them up, you know. Yeah. He pulled it like this, half into one of these coins. Oh, yeah. To wipe it out. Yeah. Yeah, it made out of this tough... Shammy skin they used sometimes. Yeah, like glass, you know, but it wasn't glass. He pulled it half into this, about that far from the metal joint. Yeah. And so he sent it back to the factory, I believe. It's a kind of a plastic stuff. Hard. Hard rubber. Yeah, yeah. The clarinet was made out of that. That's where it was. CG coin.
But the rag got stuck in the floor.

Yeah, yeah. And that pulled, but that pulled from the metal joint. It broke right there. Yeah. And so he was the fella by the name of Benny. He was to send it back. I don't know all them old boys, but me and Joe Dart, we used to work together. Pretty good how you are, Bart? Thank you, thank you. Me and Joe Dart used to work together. The clarinetist. The clarinetist. Was his name, was it Johnny Dodds or what? Yeah, Joe, he used to call him Joe. Joe. Well, he used to go on the job with his clarinet. He and them used to go together.
He's the one you say his brother was the drummer. Drummer, yeah.
The fellow, yeah. The younger one.
Yeah, baby dogs.

The drummer. Well, I used to work with him. He used to come on the job with his clarinet. I said, man, you're packing that thing all around. But were you playing a clarinet at that time? No, no. No, you were still with the violin. Yeah, yeah. I never did bother with it that time. But I just pick up on it, you know, all of a sudden, like a harmonica. Any devilish thing I put my hand on. I got a harmonica for, I don't know how long. I got two in there.
When you took up the clarinet, you didn't give up the violin then?

No, For a long while after that, I gave it up. And boys used to come here and get me, you know, to play with them, you know. But, uh, not Buddy P.T. That boy is dead. He was buried in the Gerard Cemetery. I forgot his name. But I played with several of them. The trumpet player, was it? Yeah, he was. A little light-skinned fella. I don't even forgot that boy's name.
So many of them.
Yeah, so many of them, yeah, I mixed up with. It wouldn't have been Chris Kelly. No, it wasn't Chris. I don't think he was light, was he? He was a little darker. It wasn't Chris. It wasn't Chris.
I didn't think who it would be then.

And so they wanted me to go away with them. I told them, no, I couldn't leave here. Sometimes I had to duck from them, you know. They come for me to play in different place with them, you know. It wouldn't have been Kid Rene. I believe that's the word, yeah, Kid? Kid Rene? That's the word. Because he was fairly light, I remember. Yeah, Kid Rene is right. I think it was fairly light. Oh, they want me to go with them, I... Sometime I duck them, they say, I'm coming at you tomorrow night. I say, okay. Yeah. They come, but I lied each year, you know. I checked the dude, he called, I would never answer.
They want you to play your clarinet? Play with them, yes.
Your clarinet? Yeah.
You always say, yeah. Yeah.
Play my clarinet with them. Any instrument I'd put my hand on, I'd play guitar.
Oh, I had a good...

I could play a guitar. They had a fellow once, from where I was at, a place they called Grove State. He used to come there, they had an old bridge we used to settle on, you know, at night. He said, rap? I said, what? He said, you feel like playing something with me? I said, I don't care. I said, go get your guitar, and I'll go get my guitar, you know. How darn that fellow could play a guitar though. He, you know, make that guitar say most anything. The old mule coming at the, you know, at the gate and everything. His name was Boston Penison. He was from Baton Rouge. Yeah, you could, the old mule, you know, ha, ha, ha, all that bit. Just, just, just, just like that. That guitar almost all. And me and it. And so once some fellows came around there, they said, I said, boss, no, this boy is from here. I said, yeah, he lives right across the road. So, so he said, yeah. I said, oh, no, that boy ain't from here. I said, yes, he is. And play that good? I said, that's right. He plays with me all the time. Boss, Boston was a guitar player. You could just make it talk, you know, say most anything. And I don't see him sometime.
You were speaking about the Johnny Dodds. Did you play your violin and he plays clarinet?
No, I never did play with it. Oh, you didn't play with it. No, only at work. We used to play, uh, work at a bag factory. They called Minty, Minty Bag Factory.
Oh, no, Baby Dodds told me he worked there. He bought his first drums with money he earned there.
That's why that other fellow was working too. And his brother, older brother. Yeah, brother, yeah. The clarinet player. That's right.
Worked there too.
That did.
When, when would that be about?
Oh, maybe, I'll be with 1910. That's about when Baby was working there. 1910 to 1912 along in there. Yeah, in them times, yeah.
And so, uh, they used to play together at work there?
No, he'd just bring it, you know, and go take his lesson. You know, I was never, he'd go, you know. Oh, Baby Dog, uh, this fellow too.
He'd bring it to work and then go right to his lesson. Yeah, yeah, yeah.
I see, yeah.
Oh, them boys are wonderful.
How did Dodd sound in those days on clarinet? When you first heard him, was he any good? Was he playing pretty good or?
Oh, yeah, yeah. He all was good. He was good, Johnny. I know him just like this. Him and the little one both used to work at Mintus Bag Factory.
Yeah, I didn't know the older brother worked there. I knew Baby did, yeah.
Yeah, the, the, the, the.
Baby has a picture of him sitting there on the platform. Uh-huh. See, we oughta, shoulda brought that picture. Yeah. Could be that you're on there too because I don't know who else is on there.
Well, I could be too.
You know. Next time I come, I'll bring that picture.
Yeah, I'd be so glad.
With Baby sitting there on the, uh, on the platform at lunchtime or something. Yeah. With his old clothes on, you know, working there and then just resting there.
Yeah, we used to play in a different place. Um, we played for a doctor, you know, in, uh, let me see a, not Bunky, not Bunky. Oh, shit. Let me see where Dr. Matthew was.
Yeah. In some town around here.
Lakeland, the place they call Lakeland, Louisiana. Lakeland, uh-huh. Lakeland, Louisiana. Yeah. He stayed there.
That's a pro. You mentioned, you mentioned your band played mostly for the white dancers?

White, that's right. That's right. The college, you know, the, how they want me to play, you know, the way they wanted, I didn't want to play, start that thing where they play and sell fruits, you know, if they didn't sell enough to pay us, you know, I'd charge them $35 till midnight, you know, for the whole bunch of, the college, you know. They could, we go to the white. At midnight, I'll get there, they pass their head around, you know. So they played, they played after midnight, they picked up the collection, by the way. Yeah, the collections. And everything we want. They load this little rig up with everything, you know. Yeah. Like beer they didn't, you know, country people, you know. That's, you know, beer like this people here in town. Yeah. They drink a little, leave some in the bottle, well, they give us the whole case, you know. Mm-hmm. Beer. We load it up and bring it home. Yeah. I didn't care no much, much about beer, but now I like beer. Now and then I get some beer and put it in about one or two bar cans, you know. And when I'm eating, I had a can at 12 o'clock. Mm-hmm. Yeah, I sat there and ate it with some, some green butter beans, you know. Yeah. What do you call it? A pork, not pork meat. Pickle. Oh yeah? Pickle, pickled pork. Yeah, I was hungry, I was hungry. You live here by yourself now? Yeah, by myself. I have an old girlfriend, she's very fussy, you know. And she's come, she come from Bunkie.
But she always did come here and see about me, you know.
Yeah. She was here, she used to come tonight.
She's always come, well I told the people, you know, my committees, you know.

She comes here. But sometimes I'd be sick, she take me to the hospital, not to the hospital, Dr. Goldbury. come well I told the people you know my committee you know she comes here sometimes I'd be sick she'd take me to the hospital not to the hospital Dr. Goldberg. You belong to any of the clubs or
organizations like a lot of the people do I know they? No no no just insurance yeah that barrel insurance yeah. Because there's some of them you know like the young men olympians and all that put

on parades I wondered if you ever helped them with those parades. No I remember them I remember all them were old club they used to have downtown you know. Did you ever play in any of the brass bands for the parades any place? No we was to go out once but they postponed it they asked me if I was fit I said oh hell yeah Chelsea say you ain't shaved to go out in the street no I said hell no I said I'm going to play what's up with them doing yeah I'm going to get some of them pieces I had a boy here yesterday and then he passed here to see how I was he always come around to see Mr. Ralph are you I said well I hate so much but thank goodness I'm here making out I says many done pass out I'm still here
must be here left here for some point. Did you say that you knew Joe Oliver at one time? No I didn't

I always planned to talk of it Joe Oliver but this Johnny Dodd and that little baby Dodd I know good. Remember where they lived in those days about where did they live? No I didn't I think it's uptown somewhere but I never did know. I'm not sure either I know one time baby lived up around

Louisiana that's right or near the in back of that cemetery we were talking about yeah that we were talking about yesterday he tore it down you know where the goodwill is now on Jackson he lived back of that street maybe Toledano yeah someplace up in there I think they lived most of the time yeah that's up this way yeah not so far from here yeah no it's not where did you live when you moved to the city when you

moved here to New Orleans where did you? Where I left from? No where did you live what part of the town did you live in? Oh the town oh god I came in I lived back of town on 3rd street moved from there they had this fella you know I was living right close with them uh wait let me see if I could call them uh them musicians name used to make a record back there my time white fellas on 3rd street they used to be across for me like that
Oh, I used to, oh, John, I can't call them boys' names. Yeah, they used to make records there. I know one fellow that... Let me see if he can call his name.

There's one fellow I talked to once that he used to live across from Johnny Dodds and hear the Dodds practice. I bet he heard you too. His name is Harry Shields. Remember Shields? There was a Larry Shields and a younger brother, Harry. No. They were in the original Dixieland, one of them was in the original Dixieland band. Now, he told me he heard Johnny Dodds when he was a kid. Yeah. He was here in practice up there too.
Well, this fellow, what I'm telling you, they used to make records. This one died, I believe, in California and he brought his body back this way.
Well, Larry Shields died in California. They brought him back. Yeah.
Did you have a name in mind, Mr. Robinson? Huh? Did you have a name in mind, Dad?
That's just what I'm thinking now. Shields, that's the only one I can think of. No, but they got another one. They got another one there.
Did you say buddy or something like that? No.

No, I didn't. I didn't say buddy. Let me see if I can think of them. I don't think. God, son. I don't name my tongue. And them fellas used to play. Play some music. They used to be making records, you know. How could you have?
About what year was this?
Oh, that was way back in. Yeah. Yeah.
It was Sharky made some early records with the, with the, with the, or women. It was Johnny Byersdorfer, another trumpet player. Made some early records.
I can't think of you tell the name. You know I'm good if I call the name.
Some of the New Orleans rhythm kings like Brunus brothers, but they, they live down the Irish channel.
Oh, let me see.
They made a lot of records.
I can't think of any.
Another fella's, Norman. Oh, this was right on there in the mark, though. Norman Brownlee.
Yeah, they used to make people. The year that was.
That was after you were at Mente's Bag Factory, boy.
